questions.title: Git Object Model — Blobs, Trees, Commits
questions.question: How does Git store data internally using its object model?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Git is a content-addressable filesystem — everything stored as SHA-1 hashed objects
- 4 object types: blob (file content), tree (directory listing), commit (snapshot + metadata), tag
- Blob: stores file contents — no filename, no metadata
- Tree: lists blobs and subtrees with names and permissions
- Commit: points to a tree + parent commit + author/message metadata
- Content hashing: same content = same SHA — deduplication is automatic
- .git directory: object store, refs (branches = pointers to commits), index (staging area)
- Branches are just files containing a commit SHA — extremely lightweight

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Git is fundamentally a content-addressable key-value store. Every piece of data — file content, directory structure, commit metadata — is stored as an object in .git/objects/, named by the SHA-1 hash of its content. Identical content always has the same hash, so Git never stores the same file content twice even across different commits.

The four object types form a directed acyclic graph. A blob stores raw file content. A tree is like a directory — it lists names and SHAs for blobs and other trees. A commit points to a root tree that represents the entire project snapshot, and to its parent commit. Following parent pointers from any commit traces the full history.

Branches are astonishingly simple — just a text file in .git/refs/heads/ containing the SHA of the latest commit. Creating a branch is just creating a new file with a SHA. Merging updates that file. This is why branching in Git is instantaneous — there's no copying, no heavy operation, just writing 40 characters to a file.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Object Structure

```
Commit Object: abc123
├── tree: def456            ← root directory snapshot
├── parent: a1b2c3d         ← previous commit
├── author: Alice <alice@example.com> 2024-01-15 10:00:00
└── message: feat: add payment service

Tree Object: def456
├── blob ghi789  src/PaymentService.java
├── blob jkl012  src/PaymentController.java  
└── tree mno345  src/                        ← subdirectory = subtree

Blob Object: ghi789
└── (raw content of PaymentService.java)
```

## Inspecting Git Objects

```bash
# Get the commit SHA
git log --oneline -1
# abc1234 feat: add payment service

# Inspect the commit object
git cat-file -p abc1234
# tree def456789abcdef...
# parent a1b2c3d4...
# author Alice ...
# feat: add payment service

# Inspect the tree
git cat-file -p def456789
# 100644 blob ghi789... PaymentService.java
# 100644 blob jkl012... PaymentController.java

# Inspect a blob
git cat-file -p ghi789
# (content of PaymentService.java)

# Branch is just a pointer
cat .git/refs/heads/main
# abc123456789abcdef...  (SHA of latest commit)

# HEAD points to current branch
cat .git/HEAD
# ref: refs/heads/main
```

## Content Deduplication

```
Commit 1: UserService.java → blob SHA: aaa111
Commit 2: UserService.java (unchanged) → blob SHA: aaa111  (SAME!)
          PaymentService.java (new) → blob SHA: bbb222

Git stores blob aaa111 only ONCE even though it appears in 1000 commits.
Changing one byte of UserService.java creates a new blob ccc333.
→ Git is extremely space-efficient for files that change infrequently.
```

speakable_v2.hook: Git is fundamentally a content-addressable key-value store.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is why branching in Git is instantaneous — there's no copying, no heavy operation, just writing 40 characters to a file.

questions.title: Git Hooks and Automation
questions.question: What are Git hooks and how do you use them to enforce code quality in a Java project?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Hooks: scripts that run at specific Git events (pre-commit, pre-push, commit-msg, post-merge)
- Client-side hooks: local to developer machine — .git/hooks/ directory
- pre-commit: run linting and tests before commit allowed
- commit-msg: validate commit message format (conventional commits)
- pre-push: run integration tests before push allowed
- Husky (JS) or custom scripts for sharing hooks across team
- Java: Maven/Gradle plugin to install hooks (maven-enforcer, git-commit-id-plugin)
- Server-side hooks: run on server — enforce rules for all contributors

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Git hooks are scripts that Git automatically runs at specific points in the workflow. Client-side hooks live in .git/hooks/ and enforce standards locally on each developer's machine. The most useful for a Java backend team are pre-commit for running quick checks before each commit, and commit-msg for validating that commit messages follow the conventional commits format.

The challenge with client-side hooks is sharing them — .git/hooks/ isn't committed to the repository. The common solution is to store hooks in a committed directory like .githooks/ or scripts/hooks/, and use a setup script or Maven plugin to install them. This way new team members get the hooks by running a setup command after cloning.

Server-side hooks are more powerful for enforcement. They run on the Git server and can reject pushes that violate rules — like pushes without passing CI or pushes directly to main. GitHub and GitLab implement branch protection rules on top of server-side hooks, so you usually don't need to write them yourself.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## pre-commit Hook (Checkstyle + Unit Tests)

```bash
#!/bin/sh
# .githooks/pre-commit
# Install: git config core.hooksPath .githooks

echo "Running pre-commit checks..."

# Run Checkstyle on changed files only
CHANGED_JAVA=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep '.java$')
if [ -n "$CHANGED_JAVA" ]; then
    echo "Running Checkstyle..."
    mvn checkstyle:check -q
    if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
        echo "COMMIT REJECTED: Checkstyle violations found. Run: mvn checkstyle:check"
        exit 1
    fi
fi

# Run unit tests (fast feedback)
echo "Running unit tests..."
mvn test -q -pl "$(git diff --cached --name-only | sed 's|src/.*||' | sort -u | tr '\n' ',')"
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "COMMIT REJECTED: Tests failed."
    exit 1
fi

echo "Pre-commit checks passed."
```

## commit-msg Hook (Conventional Commits)

```bash
#!/bin/sh
# .githooks/commit-msg

COMMIT_MSG=$(cat "$1")
PATTERN="^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|test|chore|perf|ci|build)(\(.+\))?(!)?: .{1,100}"

if ! echo "$COMMIT_MSG" | grep -qE "$PATTERN"; then
    echo "COMMIT REJECTED: Commit message doesn't follow conventional commits format."
    echo "Expected: type(scope): description"
    echo "Example:  feat(payments): add Stripe integration"
    echo "Example:  fix(orders): prevent duplicate order on retry"
    exit 1
fi

echo "Commit message valid."
```

## Setup Script for Team

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# scripts/setup-dev.sh — run once after cloning

# Install git hooks from committed directory
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
chmod +x .githooks/*

echo "Git hooks installed from .githooks/"
```

```xml
<!-- Maven: auto-install hooks with maven-exec-plugin -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
    <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <id>install-git-hooks</id>
            <phase>initialize</phase>
            <goals><goal>exec</goal></goals>
            <configuration>
                <executable>git</executable>
                <arguments>
                    <argument>config</argument>
                    <argument>core.hooksPath</argument>
                    <argument>.githooks</argument>
                </arguments>
            </configuration>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
```

speakable_v2.hook: Git hooks are scripts that Git automatically runs at specific points in the workflow.

questions.title: Git Submodules and Worktrees
questions.question: What are Git submodules and worktrees, and when are they useful for a Java backend project?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Submodule: embed another Git repo inside your repo — reference a specific commit
- Use case: shared library across multiple repos, keeping them versioned independently
- Submodule complexity: cloners need --recurse-submodules; updates are manual
- Modern alternative: publish shared library to Maven repo instead of submodule
- Worktree: multiple working directories from one repo — useful to work on two branches simultaneously
- git worktree add: create additional checkout without switching branches
- Use case: fix a bug while keeping feature branch changes visible
- Worktree vs stash: worktree preserves IDE state; stash is simpler for short context switches

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Submodules let you embed one Git repository inside another, pinning it to a specific commit. They're useful when multiple projects share common code and you want each project to control exactly which version of the shared code it uses. The main downside is complexity — developers need to know to clone with --recurse-submodules, and updating the submodule reference is a manual process that creates a commit in the parent repo.

For Java projects, the better pattern is usually to publish shared code as a Maven or Gradle artifact to a package registry — Nexus, Artifactory, or GitHub Packages. Consumers declare a normal dependency with a version number. This is the standard Java ecosystem approach and doesn't require any special Git knowledge.

Worktrees are more immediately useful. They let you check out different branches of the same repo into different directories simultaneously. If you're deep into feature work and need to urgently review a PR or check something in another branch, you create a worktree — a new directory pointing to the other branch — without disturbing your current working state or your IDE's open file tabs.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Git Worktrees

```bash
# On feature branch working on complex change...
git checkout feature/payment-refactor
# 20 files changed, complex state...

# Need to review a PR urgently — don't want to stash everything
# Create a worktree for the PR branch in a sibling directory
git worktree add ../review-pr-456 feature/fix-order-duplication

# Now you have:
# /projects/my-app/           ← your feature branch (unchanged)
# /projects/review-pr-456/    ← the PR branch in separate directory

# Open review directory in another IDE window or terminal
cd ../review-pr-456
# Review the code, build, test — fully independent from your feature work

# When done reviewing
cd ../my-app
git worktree remove ../review-pr-456
git branch -d feature/fix-order-duplication  # if merged
```

## Submodules (When You Really Need Them)

```bash
# Add a shared library as submodule
git submodule add https://github.com/myorg/shared-utils.git libs/shared-utils
# Creates: .gitmodules file + libs/shared-utils/ directory

# Clone with submodules
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/myorg/my-app.git
# or: git submodule update --init --recursive  (after regular clone)

# Update submodule to latest version
cd libs/shared-utils
git checkout v2.1.0  # pin to specific version
cd ..
git add libs/shared-utils
git commit -m "chore: update shared-utils to v2.1.0"
```

## Better Java Alternative — Maven Package

```xml
<!-- Instead of submodule, publish to Maven repo -->
<!-- In shared-utils pom.xml: deploy to Nexus/GitHub Packages -->
<!-- In consuming project pom.xml: -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.myorg</groupId>
    <artifactId>shared-utils</artifactId>
    <version>2.1.0</version>
</dependency>
<!-- Version controlled, cacheable, no Git complexity -->
```

speakable_v2.hook: Submodules let you embed one Git repository inside another, pinning it to a specific commit.
speakable_v2.cap: If you're deep into feature work and need to urgently review a PR or check something in another branch, you create a worktree — a new directory pointing to the other branch — without disturbing.

questions.title: Git Large Files and History Rewriting
questions.question: How do you handle large files in Git and rewrite history to remove accidentally committed secrets?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Git LFS: Git Large File Storage — stores large files externally, pointer in repo
- LFS use cases: design assets, videos, large binaries, ML models
- git filter-repo: modern tool to rewrite history (removes secret files, large binaries)
- BFG Repo Cleaner: simpler alternative for removing specific files from history
- After history rewrite: force push required (destructive — coordinate with team)
- Rotate compromised secrets immediately — removing from history doesn't revoke access
- .gitignore: prevent future accidental commits of secrets
- Pre-commit hooks: scan for secrets before commit (Gitleaks, detect-secrets)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Git stores every version of every file in its history. Large binaries — videos, compiled binaries, ML models — bloat the repository because Git can't diff them efficiently. Every clone downloads the entire history including all old versions of those files. Git LFS solves this by storing the actual file content externally (on GitHub's LFS storage or your own server) and keeping only a small pointer in Git.

Accidentally committing a secret — a database password, an API key — is a critical incident. Removing the file in a new commit doesn't help because it's still in history. Anyone with a clone has it. git filter-repo or BFG Repo Cleaner can remove the secret from all commits in history. But: you must also immediately rotate the compromised credential. Assume it's been seen. History rewriting doesn't help if it was pushed to GitHub and anyone could have read it.

Prevention is better than remediation. Pre-commit hooks with tools like Gitleaks scan staged files for patterns matching secrets before the commit is made. GitHub's secret scanning automatically alerts you when it detects known credential patterns in pushes.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Git LFS Setup

```bash
# Install and initialize
git lfs install

# Track file types in LFS
git lfs track "*.psd"   # Photoshop files
git lfs track "*.mp4"   # Videos
git lfs track "*.model" # ML models
git lfs track "*.jar"   # Compiled JARs (if needed)
# Creates .gitattributes entries — commit this file

git add .gitattributes
git commit -m "chore: configure Git LFS for large assets"

# Usage is transparent — git add/commit/push as normal
git add assets/hero-video.mp4
git commit -m "add hero video"
git push  # LFS automatically uploads binary to LFS storage

# Clone: automatic download of LFS files
git clone --recurse-submodules https://...

# View LFS tracked files
git lfs ls-files
```

## Remove Secret from History

```bash
# STEP 1: Rotate the secret IMMEDIATELY — assume it's compromised
# STEP 2: Remove from history

# Using git-filter-repo (install: pip install git-filter-repo)
git filter-repo --path secrets.properties --invert-paths
# Removes secrets.properties from ALL commits in history

# Or remove specific content pattern
git filter-repo --replace-text <(echo 'DB_PASSWORD=hunter2==>DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED')

# STEP 3: Force push (coordinate with team — they need to re-clone)
git push origin --force --all
git push origin --force --tags

# STEP 4: Tell team to re-clone (history diverged)
# Their local branches based on old history need to be rebased

# STEP 5: Add to .gitignore to prevent future accidents
echo "secrets.properties" >> .gitignore
echo "*.env" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore && git commit -m "chore: gitignore secret files"
```

## Pre-Commit Secret Detection

```bash
# Install Gitleaks
brew install gitleaks

# .githooks/pre-commit
#!/bin/sh
if gitleaks protect --staged --verbose; then
    echo "No secrets detected"
else
    echo "COMMIT REJECTED: Possible secret detected by Gitleaks"
    exit 1
fi

# Configure hook
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
chmod +x .githooks/pre-commit
```

speakable_v2.hook: Git stores every version of every file in its history.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: GitHub's secret scanning automatically alerts you when it detects known credential patterns in pushes.

questions.title: Git Tags and Semantic Versioning
questions.question: How do you use Git tags for release management and semantic versioning?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Lightweight tag: pointer to commit — just a name
- Annotated tag: object with tagger, date, message, GPG signature — preferred for releases
- Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (1.2.3)
- MAJOR: breaking API changes
- MINOR: new features, backward compatible
- PATCH: bug fixes, backward compatible
- git describe: generate version string from nearest tag
- GitHub Releases: based on tags — release notes, assets
- Automated tagging in CI: tag on merge to main, trigger release pipeline

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Annotated tags mark specific commits as important versions. Unlike lightweight tags which are just references, annotated tags contain metadata: who created them, when, and a message. They're the right choice for release tags because they provide an audit trail and can be GPG-signed for verification.

Semantic versioning is the standard for communicating the impact of a version change. MAJOR version bumps signal breaking changes — API consumers must update their code. MINOR bumps add functionality that's backward compatible — consumers can upgrade safely. PATCH bumps fix bugs without changing behavior.

For microservices that deploy continuously, version tags mark the code state for a specific deployment. When something goes wrong in production, you identify the tag in production, compare it to the current main, and have a precise understanding of what changed. Combined with the git SHA in your Docker image tag, you have complete traceability from a running container back to the exact source code.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Working with Tags

```bash
# Create annotated release tag
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release 1.2.0 — add payment gateway integration"
git push origin v1.2.0

# Create lightweight tag (for dev use, not releases)
git tag v1.2.0-rc1

# List tags
git tag                    # all tags
git tag -l 'v1.*'          # filter by pattern
git tag --sort=-v:refname  # sorted by semantic version, descending

# Show tag details
git show v1.2.0

# Delete tag
git tag -d v1.2.0              # delete local
git push origin :refs/tags/v1.2.0  # delete remote

# Checkout tag (for investigation — creates detached HEAD)
git checkout v1.1.0

# git describe: version string from tag
git describe --tags --always
# v1.2.0       ← exact tag
# v1.2.0-3-gabc1234  ← 3 commits after v1.2.0, SHA abc1234
```

## Semantic Versioning Rules

```
Given version MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH:

Increment MAJOR when you make incompatible API changes:
  1.2.3 → 2.0.0
  Example: rename endpoint, change response schema, remove field

Increment MINOR when you add backward-compatible features:
  1.2.3 → 1.3.0
  Example: add new endpoint, add optional field to response

Increment PATCH when you make backward-compatible bug fixes:
  1.2.3 → 1.2.4
  Example: fix NPE, correct calculation, improve error message

Pre-release: 1.3.0-SNAPSHOT, 1.3.0-rc.1, 1.3.0-beta.2
```

## Automated Release Tagging (GitHub Actions)

```yaml
# On push to main — auto-tag and create GitHub Release
- name: Create release tag
  run: |
    VERSION=$(cat VERSION)  # or from pom.xml
    git tag -a "v${VERSION}" -m "Release v${VERSION}"
    git push origin "v${VERSION}"

- name: Create GitHub Release
  uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v1
  if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/')
  with:
    generate_release_notes: true  # auto-generate from commit messages
    files: target/app.jar
```

speakable_v2.hook: Annotated tags mark specific commits as important versions.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Combined with the git SHA in your Docker image tag, you have complete traceability from a running container back to the exact source code.

questions.title: Monorepo vs Multirepo Strategy
questions.question: What are the trade-offs between monorepo and multirepo for Java microservices?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Monorepo: all services in one repo — atomic cross-service commits, easier refactoring
- Multirepo: one repo per service — independent versioning, isolated CI, loose coupling
- Monorepo tools: Nx, Turborepo, Gradle composite builds, Bazel for large scale
- Selective CI: only build changed services (affected module detection)
- Code sharing: monorepo makes sharing libraries trivial; multirepo requires publishing
- Ownership: CODEOWNERS per directory in monorepo; repo-level access in multirepo
- Google/Facebook: extreme monorepo at scale; most teams: multirepo or moderate monorepo
- Practical: 2-10 services → monorepo; 20+ services → multirepo or structured monorepo

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A monorepo keeps all microservices in a single repository. Atomic commits can span multiple services — when you change a shared interface and update all consumers, that's one commit, one PR, one review. Refactoring that touches many services is straightforward. Code sharing via a common module is trivial.

The challenges with monorepo at scale are CI performance and repository size. If you run the full build on every commit, and the repo has 20 services, most services are building and testing code that didn't change. Tools like selective CI — only build services that had files changed — mitigate this.

Multirepo gives each service its own deployment lifecycle, CI pipeline, and permissions boundary. Teams can evolve their service independently without coordinating with others. But cross-service changes require coordinated PRs across multiple repos. Shared libraries require publishing to a package registry. For teams of 5-10 engineers working on 3-5 services, monorepo usually wins on simplicity. For 50+ engineers on 30+ services, multirepo or tooled monorepo becomes necessary.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Monorepo Structure

```
my-company/
├── services/
│   ├── order-service/      ← own pom.xml, Dockerfile, CI config
│   ├── payment-service/
│   ├── user-service/
│   └── notification-service/
├── shared/
│   ├── common-events/      ← shared Kafka event schemas
│   ├── common-dto/         ← shared DTOs for API contracts
│   └── test-utils/         ← shared test helpers
├── infrastructure/
│   ├── terraform/
│   └── helm-charts/
├── .github/
│   └── CODEOWNERS          ← per-directory ownership
└── pom.xml                 ← parent POM
```

## Selective CI (Only Build Changed)

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  detect-changes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      order-service: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.order-service }}
      payment-service: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.payment-service }}
    steps:
      - uses: dorny/paths-filter@v2
        id: filter
        with:
          filters: |
            order-service:
              - 'services/order-service/**'
              - 'shared/**'   # shared changes affect all services
            payment-service:
              - 'services/payment-service/**'
              - 'shared/**'

  build-order-service:
    needs: detect-changes
    if: needs.detect-changes.outputs.order-service == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: mvn -pl services/order-service -am package

  build-payment-service:
    needs: detect-changes
    if: needs.detect-changes.outputs.payment-service == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: mvn -pl services/payment-service -am package
```

## CODEOWNERS in Monorepo

```
# .github/CODEOWNERS

# Default: all changes reviewed by architects
*                              @architects-team

# Service-specific ownership
/services/order-service/       @order-team
/services/payment-service/     @payment-team @security-team
/shared/common-events/         @architects-team  # API contracts need architect review
/infrastructure/               @devops-team
```

speakable_v2.hook: A monorepo keeps all microservices in a single repository.
speakable_v2.cap: For 50+ engineers on 30+ services, multirepo or tooled monorepo becomes necessary.

questions.question: When should you use git merge versus git rebase in a Java backend project?
questions.title: Git merge vs rebase — when to use each
questions.direct_answer: Use merge to preserve the full history of parallel development and for integrating long-lived feature branches into main. Use rebase to produce a cleaner, linear commit history on short-lived topic branches before merging, or to keep a feature branch up-to-date with main without introducing merge commits.
questions.interviewer_intent: Assesses understanding of Git history management, team workflow conventions, and the trade-offs between readability and traceability in collaborative Java projects.

sections.title: Two Ways to Integrate Work — and Why History Shape Matters at 2 AM
sections.content:
Every Git team eventually fights about this: merge or rebase? The debate feels religious, but the real decision is structural — it determines what `git log` looks like and how you investigate production incidents.

**Merge** creates a new commit that joins two branch tips, preserving every commit in its original form and maintaining the full directed acyclic graph of parallel development. When you look at history, you see exactly when two lines of work converged. **Rebase** replays your commits on top of a new base, rewriting SHA hashes to produce a clean linear sequence — as if the work happened in order on a single branch.

The consequence shows up during an incident at 2 AM. Merge history lets you pinpoint exactly when a feature was integrated — the merge commit maps to a specific PR and review. Linear rebase history makes `git bisect` faster because there are no merge commits confusing the binary search. Neither is universally better; your team's deployment model, compliance requirements, and review workflow determine which shape serves you.

The golden rule that prevents disasters: never rebase commits that have been pushed to a branch someone else has pulled. Violating this forces teammates into `git reset --hard` recovery — and in a busy Java backend team, that means lost work.

sections.title: The Core Trade-offs: Merge vs Rebase Side by Side
sections.content:
The differences are not just cosmetic — they affect safety, tooling, and team workflows in concrete ways.

| Dimension | git merge | git rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History shape | Non-linear DAG with merge commits | Linear chain of commits |
| Original SHAs preserved | Yes — nothing is rewritten | No — every replayed commit gets a new hash |
| Safe on shared branches | Always safe — adds a commit | Dangerous — requires force-push |
| Conflict resolution | Resolved once at merge time | May need resolution per replayed commit |
| `git bisect` friendliness | Merge commits can confuse the search | Clean linear history is ideal for bisect |
| Audit trail | Exact record of when branches converged | Looks clean but the timeline is synthetic |
| CI/CD integration | Merge commit is a natural deployment gate | Requires discipline to not rebase after push |
| Ideal use case | Integrating completed features into main | Cleaning up a feature branch before PR |

sections.title: The Decision Framework: Match the Tool to the Branch Lifecycle
sections.content:
The decision comes down to two questions: is this branch shared, and what story does the team need from history?

For **integrating completed features into main**, merge is almost always correct. The merge commit becomes a clear milestone — one commit that maps to one pull request, one code review, one deployment decision. This is especially valuable in regulated Java backend environments where audit trails matter. If something breaks in production, `git log --merges` gives you the timeline of every integration event.

For **keeping a feature branch current** during active development, rebase onto main daily. This produces a clean diff for reviewers and avoids the noise of upstream merge commits cluttering your branch. But stop rebasing the moment someone else pulls your branch.

The **squash-and-merge hybrid** is increasingly popular in microservice teams. Each PR collapses into a single commit on main regardless of how many WIP commits existed during development. You get the cleanest possible main history at the cost of losing individual commit attribution within a feature. Configure GitHub to append the PR number (`#123`) in the squash commit message so the detailed history remains accessible through the PR page.

The trap teams fall into: debating merge vs rebase on every PR instead of encoding the decision in branch protection rules. Pick a convention, enforce it with CI gates, and stop relitigating during code review.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Merge preserves the full DAG with original SHAs** — creates a merge commit recording exactly when branches converged, giving audit-quality history for incident review and compliance traceability
- **Rebase rewrites every replayed commit's SHA** — produces linear history ideal for `git bisect`, but breaks references anyone else holds to the original commits
- **Never rebase a pushed shared branch** — teammates who pulled the old history face diverged refs and must `git reset --hard`, which risks lost uncommitted work across the team
- **`--force-with-lease` is the safety net** — unlike `--force`, it checks that the remote branch hasn't moved since your last fetch, preventing silent overwrites of a teammate's emergency hotfix
- **Squash-and-merge is the modern hybrid** — each PR collapses into one commit on main giving clean history, but loses per-commit attribution; append the PR number in the message to preserve traceability

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Merge and rebase both integrate changes from one branch into another — the code result is identical. The difference is entirely in what `git log` looks like afterward and whether history is ever rewritten.

**Merge — preserving honest history**
- Merge creates a merge commit that records exactly when the feature branch entered the main branch — during an incident, that bookmark tells you which commit introduced a change and when
- Fast-forward merges skip the merge commit when the branch is linear, but the default `--no-ff` flag keeps it, making integrations visible in the graph
- Merge never rewrites pushed history, which makes it safe to use on any shared branch without coordinating with teammates

**Rebase — rewriting for a cleaner story**
- Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing a linear history as though the feature was developed after all main-branch changes — reviewers see purposeful commits, not tangled WIP entries mixed with upstream merges
- The critical rule: never rebase a branch that others have checked out — replaying commits produces new SHAs, and a force-push after rebase silently overwrites any commits your teammates added on top of the old SHAs
- Use `--force-with-lease` instead of `--force` when pushing after a rebase — it checks that no one pushed to the remote branch while you were rebasing and fails safely if they did

**Squash-and-merge — the practical compromise**
- Squash-and-merge collapses the entire PR into one commit on main, attaching the PR number — you get linear history without the discipline of clean individual commits throughout development
- The trade-off: `git bisect` and `git blame` become less precise since the full development history is collapsed; for a PR that touched ten files it can be harder to isolate which change introduced a bug

Pick one convention, encode it in branch protection rules, and stop re-deciding it in every code review.

questions.question: How does Git Flow compare to trunk-based development, and which suits a Java backend team?
questions.title: Git flow vs trunk-based development
questions.direct_answer: Git Flow structures work around long-lived branches (feature, develop, release, hotfix, main) and suits teams with scheduled release cycles. Trunk-based development has everyone integrate into a single main branch multiple times per day using feature flags and short-lived branches, enabling continuous delivery. Most modern Java backend teams with CI/CD pipelines favor trunk-based development.
questions.interviewer_intent: Probes knowledge of branching strategies, CI/CD maturity, and the ability to align version control practices with deployment frequency and team size.

sections.title: The Real Question: Can Your Team Ship from main Every Day?
sections.content:
Git Flow was designed in 2010 for a world where software shipped in versioned releases with explicit freeze periods. It prescribes a strict branch topology — `develop` accumulates features, `release/*` branches stabilize them, `hotfix/*` patches production, and `main` holds only released code. **Trunk-based development** (TBD) flips this entirely: all developers integrate into a single trunk multiple times per day, hiding incomplete work behind feature flags rather than branches.

The choice is not academic — it determines your deployment frequency, merge conflict rate, and CI pipeline architecture. Git Flow's extra branches create ceremony that protects against half-baked releases but slows velocity. Trunk-based development eliminates that ceremony in exchange for demanding a fast, reliable test suite and disciplined feature flagging. Without those prerequisites, TBD just means deploying broken code.

In practice, the decision comes down to whether your Spring services can ship from `main` daily. If your CI runs in under 15 minutes and your team has feature flag infrastructure, trunk-based is the natural choice. If you must freeze `release/*` branches for contractual drops or maintain multiple supported versions simultaneously, Git Flow's structure still earns its complexity.

sections.title: Git Flow vs Trunk-Based: Where They Actually Differ
sections.content:
The comparison reveals that the strategies optimize for fundamentally different deployment models — scheduled releases versus continuous delivery.

| Dimension | Git Flow | Trunk-Based Development |
|---|---|---|
| Long-lived branches | develop, release/*, hotfix/* | Only main — feature branches live 1–2 days max |
| Release cadence | Scheduled / versioned releases | Deploy on every merge to main |
| Feature flags required | No — branches hide incomplete work | Essential — in-progress code is on main |
| CI pipeline complexity | Must run on multiple long-lived branches | Single integration point simplifies CI |
| Merge conflict risk | High — branches diverge over days/weeks | Low — small, frequent integrations |
| Hotfix process | Dedicated hotfix branch merged to main + develop | Patch main directly, redeploy immediately |
| Team onboarding | More rules and branch types to learn | Simpler mental model, fewer ceremonies |

sections.title: The CI/CD Pipeline Shape Changes With Your Branching Model
sections.content:
Misalignment between branching strategy and pipeline architecture is one of the most common sources of deployment friction in Java backend teams. The branching model dictates how your pipeline must be structured.

For **trunk-based development**, the pipeline is straightforward: every merge to `main` triggers build, test, and deploy to staging. Promotion to production uses a manual approval gate or a canary deployment that auto-promotes after health checks pass. The pipeline must be fast — under 15 minutes for build and test combined — because it runs on every merge. Invest in Gradle build cache, test parallelization, and selective test execution that only runs tests affected by changed modules.

For **Git Flow**, the pipeline fans out across branches. The `develop` branch deploys to a dev environment, `release/*` branches deploy to staging with full regression suites, and merges to `main` deploy to production. The hidden cost is the **hotfix dual-merge problem**: a hotfix branch must merge to both `main` and `develop`. Forgetting the `develop` merge means the fix disappears on the next release cut. Automate this with a GitHub Action that creates a PR to `develop` whenever a hotfix merges to `main`.

The pragmatic middle ground most Java teams land on is **scaled trunk-based**: short-lived feature branches (one to two days) merged via PR after a green CI build. This gives you the code-review gate without weeks-long branch divergence.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Git Flow optimizes for versioned, scheduled releases** — the `develop` / `release/*` / `hotfix/*` topology makes sense when you must freeze code, run week-long QA cycles, or support multiple deployed versions simultaneously
- **Trunk-based optimizes for continuous delivery** — everyone integrates into `main` frequently, hiding incomplete work behind feature flags; this demands a fast test suite (under 15 minutes) or you're deploying broken code
- **Git Flow's hidden cost is the hotfix dual-merge** — a hotfix must merge to both `main` and `develop`; forgetting the `develop` merge means the fix vanishes on the next release cut, a silent regression
- **Merge conflict risk scales with branch age** — Git Flow branches diverge for days or weeks, making Java refactors across packages painful; trunk-based keeps diffs small and merge conflicts rare
- **Scaled trunk-based is the pragmatic middle** — short-lived feature branches (1–2 days) plus protected `main` gives review gates without Git Flow's heavyweight topology

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Git Flow and trunk-based development are both valid branching strategies — the right choice depends on how your team ships and whether you must maintain multiple deployed versions simultaneously.

**Git Flow — structured release management**
- Git Flow works around two long-lived branches: `main` holds production code and `develop` accumulates features; release branches stabilize a version before it merges to main
- Built for teams that ship versioned releases on a schedule — the `release/*` branch gives a freeze window for QA without blocking new feature work on `develop`
- The hotfix dual-merge trap catches most teams eventually: a `hotfix/*` branch must merge to both `main` and `develop`; skip the `develop` merge and the fix silently disappears when the next release is cut

**Trunk-based development — continuous integration as a practice**
- Everyone integrates small, complete changes to main (or a short-lived branch measured in hours) — the merge conflict rate drops because branches diverge for a day, not weeks
- Incomplete features hide behind feature flags rather than long-lived branches, which decouples deployment from release — you ship code to production before the feature is user-facing
- Requires a fast CI pipeline and a culture of green builds; a broken main blocks everyone, so the feedback loop must be short enough that developers fix it immediately

**How to choose**
- Trunk-based is the right default for most Java backend teams: fewer conflicts, faster integration, and a forcing function for small commits
- Git Flow is justified when the team contractually supports multiple deployed versions — B2B SaaS customers on staggered upgrade schedules, libraries that maintain multiple minor version branches

Invest in feature flag infrastructure before adopting trunk-based — it is the mechanism that makes incomplete features safe to deploy.

questions.question: How do you resolve merge conflicts effectively in a Java backend codebase?
questions.title: How to resolve merge conflicts effectively
questions.direct_answer: Resolve merge conflicts by first understanding both sides of the change, using a three-way diff tool to compare ancestor, ours, and theirs, then making a deliberate editorial decision. In Java codebases, the most common conflicts occur in import blocks, dependency files (pom.xml/build.gradle), and auto-generated sources. Automated pre-merge practices — rebasing frequently and keeping PRs small — reduce conflict frequency dramatically.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests practical day-to-day Git proficiency, communication skills around collaboration, and knowledge of tooling available for Java projects.

sections.title: Why Understanding Intent Matters More Than Picking a Side
sections.content:
A merge conflict is not an error — it is Git telling you that two humans made decisions about the same code, and a third human (you) needs to make the editorial call. The mistake most developers make is treating conflicts as an annoyance to dismiss quickly: accept mine, accept theirs, done. That reflex silently drops features, introduces duplicate logic, or creates compile errors that only surface in CI twenty minutes later.

The real skill is **reading intent before touching markers**. A conflict in `UserService.java` means nothing without knowing that one branch added OAuth support while the other refactored session management. Blindly picking one side deletes the other feature entirely. Java codebases have specific conflict hotspots that make this worse: auto-sorted import blocks produce spurious conflicts, `pom.xml` version strings collide when two branches bump different dependencies, and Lombok-generated code creates diffs in files nobody actually edited.

The three-way merge view — showing the common ancestor alongside both branches — is the single most important tool. It turns an ambiguous two-way diff into a clear picture of what each side intended to change relative to the original.

sections.title: Read Both Sides Before Editing Any Marker
sections.content:
Before opening the conflicted file, run `git log --merge -p <file>` to see the commits from both branches that touched this file. Read the commit messages — they explain *why* each change was made. A conflict between "add retry logic to payment call" and "extract payment call to separate service" requires combining both changes, not picking one.

In **IntelliJ IDEA**, use the built-in three-way merge dialog (Git → Resolve Conflicts). It shows the common ancestor in the center, your version on the left, their version on the right, and lets you cherry-pick hunks from either side into the result. This is dramatically more effective than reading raw `<<<<<<<` markers in a text editor, especially for Java files where the conflict spans method boundaries.

For `pom.xml` dependency conflicts, don't arbitrarily pick one version. Check Maven Central for the newest compatible version of the dependency. If both branches bumped different libraries, you likely need both changes — take the union of additions. The test in the next step will catch any incompatibilities immediately.

sections.title: Compile and Test Immediately — Don't Trust Your Edit
sections.content:
After resolving every conflicted file, run `mvn compile` or `./gradlew compileJava` before doing anything else. This catches two classes of problems instantly: stray **conflict markers** (`<<<<<<<`) that cause cryptic parse errors, and broken imports from missing or duplicate lines that Java's strict compilation rules will flag immediately.

Then run the test suite: `mvn test`. A merge resolution that compiles but breaks a test is worse than one that fails to compile — the compile failure is obvious, but a silent behavioral regression can reach production. Pay special attention to tests that exercise the code paths modified by *both* branches, since that is exactly where your editorial decision could have been wrong.

Once tests pass, stage with `git add <files>` and commit with `git commit`. Git pre-populates the merge message describing which branches were merged. Augment it with a note about non-trivial resolutions: "Resolved UserService conflict by combining OAuth support from feature/auth with session refactor from feature/sessions." Future engineers reading `git blame` will thank you for that context.

sections.title: Prevent Conflicts Before They Happen
sections.content:
The best conflict resolution strategy is reducing conflict frequency. Two practices cut conflict rates by roughly 80% in busy Java backend teams.

First, **rebase your feature branch onto main daily** rather than waiting until merge time. A one-day divergence produces small, manageable conflicts. A one-week divergence produces cascading conflicts across files where the context has shifted so much that the three-way merge loses its usefulness.

Second, **keep PRs under 400 lines of change**. Large PRs touch more files, increasing the probability of overlap with concurrent work. A PR that changes 50 files has a near-certain chance of conflicting with someone else's work on a team of ten. A PR that changes 5 files rarely conflicts.

For Java-specific sources of spurious conflicts, configure consistent import ordering via `.editorconfig` or Checkstyle rules so the formatter never produces diffs in import blocks. Use `.gitattributes` with `merge=union` for purely additive files like `CHANGELOG.md` where both sides' additions are always valid. For `pom.xml` version conflicts, centralize dependency versions in a `<dependencyManagement>` block in a parent POM — branches that add dependencies reference the managed version rather than specifying their own, eliminating the most common source of XML merge conflicts.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Read intent before resolving markers** — `git log --merge -p <file>` plus commit messages explain why both sides touched the same code; blindly accepting one side silently drops the other feature
- **Three-way merge is the essential tool** — IntelliJ's ancestor + ours + theirs view makes `pom.xml` and service-layer conflicts legible; raw marker editing in a text editor is error-prone
- **Compile immediately after resolution** — `mvn compile` catches stray `<<<<<<<` markers and broken imports in seconds, before they waste 20 minutes in CI
- **Rebase daily, PR under 400 lines** — one-day divergence produces small conflicts; one-week divergence produces cascading conflicts where context has shifted beyond three-way merge usefulness
- **`.gitattributes merge=union` for additive files** — eliminates spurious conflicts in changelogs and other append-only files where both sides' additions are always valid

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A merge conflict means two branches modified the same code in incompatible ways. The instinct to immediately edit conflict markers is the wrong first move — understanding why both sides touched the same code tells you which changes should survive.

**Understanding the conflict before editing**
- Run `git log --merge` before touching conflict markers to see which commits on each side modified the conflicting files — a conflict in a service class often means two features changed the same method, and blindly picking one side silently deletes the other
- Three-way merge tools (IntelliJ's merge dialog, VS Code's diff editor) show the common ancestor alongside both branches — resolving hunks individually is safer than picking entire sides wholesale
- For `pom.xml` conflicts, always resolve manually — take the union of both additions and verify compatibility against Maven Central; automated tools often discard one team's dependency silently

**After resolving — verification before committing**
- Run `mvn compile` immediately after resolving Java file conflicts — stray conflict markers cause cryptic parse errors, and broken imports from duplicate lines fail compilation before they waste test time
- Run the full test suite before pushing the resolution — a conflict resolution that compiles but breaks tests has introduced a regression under the appearance of a clean merge
- Use `git diff HEAD` to review what the final resolved state looks like as a whole before committing — conflicts in multiple files can interact in non-obvious ways

**Prevention — the best conflict is the one that never happens**
- Rebase onto main daily during active development to minimize divergence; PRs under 400 lines conflict far less often than large PRs
- Enforce consistent import ordering via Checkstyle or Spotless so the formatter never produces spurious diffs in import blocks that cause false conflicts
- Communicate intent before making large structural refactors — a team-wide rename or package reorganization should be a coordinated commit, not a PR that collides with everyone else's work

questions.question: How do you use git interactive rebase to squash and edit commits before merging a feature branch?
questions.title: Git interactive rebase — squashing and editing commits
questions.direct_answer: Use `git rebase -i <base>` to open an editor listing every commit since the branch diverged. Mark commits with `squash` or `fixup` to fold them into a predecessor, `reword` to change a message, or `drop` to remove a commit entirely. The result is a polished, reviewable commit sequence before the branch is merged.
questions.interviewer_intent: Evaluates Git fluency beyond basic commands and the candidate's commitment to commit hygiene, which correlates with collaborative professionalism.

sections.title: Your Commit History Is a Story — Interactive Rebase Is the Editing Phase
sections.content:
During development, you commit freely — "WIP", "fix null check", "forgot test", "actually fix the test" — because frequent commits give you a safety net. But those commits are not the story you want reviewers, `git blame` users, or future archaeologists to read. **Interactive rebase** is the editing phase that transforms raw working history into a clean narrative.

`git rebase -i` opens a TODO list of commits since your branch diverged, each prefixed with a verb. You control the fate of every commit: `pick` keeps it, `squash` folds it into the previous commit and combines messages, `fixup` folds it silently (discarding the message), `reword` lets you change the message, `edit` pauses so you can amend or split, and `drop` removes it entirely. Git replays the commits in order, applying your edits.

The key mental model: interactive rebase is not changing code — it is reshaping how the same changes are packaged into commits. The final working tree after rebasing is identical to before. Only the commit boundaries and messages change. This makes it safe for unpushed work and dangerous for pushed work, because anyone who has the old commits will see them diverge from your rewritten ones.

sections.title: Set Up the Session and Read the TODO List Before Editing
sections.content:
Start with `git rebase -i origin/main` to rebase against the remote main branch, or `git rebase -i HEAD~N` to target the last N commits. Git opens your `$EDITOR` with the TODO list — commits listed oldest-first, each on a line like `pick abc1234 add user service`.

Before changing any verbs, **read the full list and plan the result**. Decide which commits represent logical units of work that a reviewer should step through. A good rule: each surviving commit should be one complete, self-contained idea — one for the domain model change, one for the service layer, one for the REST controller. Everything else (`fix typo`, `WIP`, `address review comment`) should be folded into its parent with `fixup`.

The setup for a typical Java feature branch looks like this — five WIP commits being condensed into two meaningful ones:

```
pick abc1234 feat(auth): add JWT token generation
fixup def5678 fix: null check on claims
fixup ghi9012 WIP: add test
pick jkl3456 feat(auth): add token refresh endpoint
fixup mno7890 fix: correct expiry calculation
```

After saving and closing the editor, Git replays each commit according to the verbs. The result is two clean commits that tell a clear story.

sections.title: Handle Conflicts, Split Commits, and Use the Autosquash Shortcut
sections.content:
During replay, Git may hit conflicts — the same resolution process as a normal rebase applies. Resolve the conflict, run `git add`, then `git rebase --continue`. At any point, `git rebase --abort` returns the branch to its exact original state with no damage done.

The **edit** verb unlocks commit splitting — mark a commit as `edit`, and Git pauses after applying it. Run `git reset HEAD^` to unstage the commit's changes, then selectively stage subsets with `git add -p` and create separate commits. This is invaluable in Java codebases when a single commit accidentally mixed a rename refactor with a behavior change — splitting them makes `git bisect` dramatically more useful because a test failure bisects to the behavior change, not the mixed commit.

The **autosquash workflow** eliminates manual reordering entirely. During development, when you notice a bug in an earlier commit, create a fixup commit targeting it: `git commit --fixup=abc1234`. This creates a commit with the message `fixup! add JWT token generation`. Later, `git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main` automatically positions fixup commits next to their targets and marks them as `fixup`. Set `git config --global rebase.autoSquash true` to enable this by default on every interactive rebase.

sections.title: Force-Push Safely — The Difference Between --force and --force-with-lease
sections.content:
Because interactive rebase rewrites commit SHAs, you must force-push to update the remote branch: `git push --force-with-lease origin feature/auth`. The `--force-with-lease` flag is critical — it checks that no one else has pushed commits to the remote branch since your last fetch. If someone has, the push is rejected, preventing you from silently overwriting their work.

Never use bare `--force` on a branch that anyone else might have pulled. The difference is concrete: **`--force` overwrites unconditionally**, while `--force-with-lease` refuses if the remote ref has moved. On a team where two engineers share a feature branch, `--force` after a rebase can destroy the other engineer's commits without any warning.

After pushing, update the PR description to reflect the rebased commit structure. Teammates who had locally checked out your branch need to run `git fetch && git reset --hard origin/feature/auth` to sync — notify them in the PR comments. Add a CI check that scans PR commit messages for `fixup!` or `squash!` prefixes to ensure no developer submits a PR with un-squashed fixup commits still visible.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`git rebase -i` is a history editor, not a code editor** — the final working tree is identical before and after; only commit boundaries and messages change, making it safe for unpushed work
- **`fixup` vs `squash`** — `fixup` folds changes and discards the message (ideal for "fix typo" commits); `squash` keeps the combined messages for you to edit into one coherent description
- **`edit` enables commit splitting** — pause at a commit, `git reset HEAD^` to unstage, then `git add -p` to create separate logical commits; invaluable when a Java refactor accidentally mixed renaming with behavior changes
- **`--force-with-lease` prevents silent overwrites** — refuses to push if the remote branch has moved since your last fetch, catching the case where a teammate pushed an emergency fix you're about to destroy
- **`git commit --fixup=<sha>` plus `--autosquash`** — creates fixup commits during development that automatically position themselves next to their targets during interactive rebase, eliminating manual reordering

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Interactive rebase is a history cleanup tool used immediately before opening or updating a PR — during development you commit freely, but the commits reviewers see should tell a coherent story about what the feature does.

**The typical workflow**
- `git rebase -i origin/main` opens the interactive editor listing every commit since the branch diverged; commits are shown oldest-first, opposite of `git log`
- Mark well-scoped commits as `pick` and everything else as `fixup` — fixup squashes the commit into the previous pick without preserving its message; `squash` lets you combine and edit the message
- The goal: three to five logical commits where each represents one complete idea — the domain model, the service layer, the controller — so reviewers can step through the feature's evolution rather than a stream of "WIP" and "fix null check"

**Safety practices**
- Always use `--force-with-lease` instead of `--force` when pushing after a rebase — it checks that no one pushed to the remote branch while you were rebasing; bare `--force` silently overwrites any commits they added
- Never interactive-rebase a branch that others have checked out — replaying commits produces new SHA1 hashes, making the remote branch incompatible with any local checkout based on the original SHAs
- Set `rebase.autoSquash true` globally — then `git commit --fixup <sha>` creates a commit that interactive rebase automatically places and squashes below the referenced commit

**Advanced: splitting a commit with `edit`**
- Mark a commit as `edit` to pause the rebase at that point; run `git reset HEAD^` to unstage everything, then recommit in separate logical units
- Useful when a rename and a behavior change were accidentally committed together — splitting them makes `git bisect` pinpoint bugs more precisely and makes `git blame` more informative

questions.question: When backporting a bug fix to a maintenance branch, should you use cherry-pick, merge, or rebase?
questions.title: Cherry-pick vs merge vs rebase for backporting fixes
questions.direct_answer: Cherry-pick is almost always the right tool for backporting: it copies one or more specific commits to a target branch without bringing along unrelated changes. Merge would pull in the entire branch history, and rebase would replay all commits since the divergence point — both are too broad for a targeted backport. Reserve merge and rebase for integrating full feature work.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests knowledge of selective change propagation, maintenance branch management, and the real-world scenario of supporting multiple deployed versions of a Java service.

sections.title: Backporting Needs a Scalpel, Not a Sledgehammer
sections.content:
Backporting means taking a fix from the main development line and applying it to an older release branch still running in production. Java services in enterprises commonly run multiple concurrent versions — a `v2.x` branch on long-term support while `v3.x` carries active development. The challenge is applying *only* the fix without dragging along months of unrelated features.

This is where the three Git propagation tools — **cherry-pick**, **merge**, and **rebase** — diverge sharply. Cherry-pick copies specific commits to a target branch without touching anything else. Merge pulls in the entire source branch history since divergence. Rebase replays every commit since the branches split, rewriting SHAs along the way. For a targeted backport, only cherry-pick gives you the surgical precision needed.

The common mistake is reaching for merge out of habit. Merge works beautifully for integrating completed features, but when you merge `main` into `v2.x`, you pull in every commit since the branch point — three months of new features dumped into what is supposed to be a stable, minimal maintenance release. That violates the entire purpose of a maintenance branch.

sections.title: Cherry-pick vs Merge vs Rebase for Targeted Backports
sections.content:
Each tool propagates changes differently, and the differences are consequential when maintaining stable release branches alongside active development.

| Dimension | cherry-pick | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|---|
| Selectivity | Copies specific commits only | Brings entire branch history | Replays all commits since divergence |
| SHA preservation | New SHA on target branch | No rewrite — merge commit added | Rewrites all replayed SHAs |
| Safe on shared branch | Yes — only adds commits | Yes | No — requires force-push |
| Risk of pulling in unrelated features | None — only selected commits travel | High — entire source branch merged | High — all commits replayed |
| Audit traceability | Use `-x` flag to record source SHA | Merge commit links both histories | No automatic link to original |
| Automation support | GitHub/GitLab backport bots available | Manual process | Manual process |

sections.title: The Cherry-pick Workflow: From Fix to Backport in Three Commands
sections.content:
The practical workflow for backporting a security fix from `main` to `release/2.x` starts with identifying the **exact commit SHA** on main that contains the fix. Use `git log --oneline main` or find the merge commit of the PR that delivered the fix.

Switch to the maintenance branch and cherry-pick with the `-x` flag. The `-x` flag appends the source SHA to the commit message, creating an audit trail that links the backport to its origin.

```bash
git checkout release/2.x
git cherry-pick -x abc1234
# -x appends "(cherry picked from commit abc1234)" to the message
```

This **traceability** is critical in regulated industries — fintech, healthcare, government — where you need to prove that a CVE fix was applied to every supported release. The `-x` annotation in the commit message creates that audit trail without any additional tooling.

If the cherry-pick conflicts because the surrounding code has diverged on the maintenance branch, resolve the conflict manually. Sometimes the fix depends on a refactor that only exists on main. In that case, you have two options: cherry-pick the refactor commit first (in order), or write a standalone fix specifically for the `v2.x` code context. The standalone fix is usually safer because it avoids pulling in refactoring assumptions that may not hold on the older branch.

After resolving, run the full test suite against the maintenance branch to verify the fix works in the older codebase context — dependencies, APIs, and framework versions may differ from main.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cherry-pick is surgical** — copies selected commits to another branch without dragging unrelated mainline history; the only appropriate tool for backporting CVE fixes to `release/2.x`
- **Merge backports the whole branch** — merging `main` into a maintenance branch pulls every commit since divergence, dumping months of new features into a stable release and violating its purpose
- **Rebase is never the right backport tool** — it replays the entire commit range since divergence and rewrites SHAs, forcing a disruptive force-push on a shared maintenance branch
- **`-x` flag creates an audit breadcrumb** — appends the original SHA to the cherry-picked commit message so compliance teams can trace a security patch across every supported release branch
- **Dependency chains require ordered cherry-picks** — if a fix depends on a refactor absent from the old branch, cherry-pick both in order or write a standalone fix for the older code context

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Backporting a bug fix to a maintenance branch requires copying a specific commit without bringing along unrelated history. Cherry-pick is the right tool for this — the other two options bring far more than you want.

**Cherry-pick — surgical backporting**
- `git cherry-pick -x <sha>` copies one specific commit to the current branch and appends the original SHA to the commit message — the `-x` creates a traceable link from the maintenance branch commit back to the main-branch source
- Cherry-pick is correct when the fix is a single, well-scoped commit on main; if the fix spans multiple commits, cherry-pick them in order so the branch compiles at each step
- When the target branch diverges enough that the patch does not apply cleanly, write a standalone fix for the older context rather than importing assumptions from main that do not hold there

**Why not merge for backporting**
- Merging `main` into `v2.x` brings three months of new features, API changes, and dependency upgrades along with the one security fix — the maintenance branch loses its purpose of being a stable, minimal surface
- Merge commits also obscure what was actually ported, making audit trails harder to produce for security teams

**Why not rebase for backporting**
- Rebase replays every commit since the branch diverged — on a maintenance branch that split six months ago, that could be hundreds of commits replayed onto a codebase with different structure
- Rebase rewrites SHAs and requires a force-push on a shared branch that other engineers have checked out

The key enabling practice: keeping commits on main small and logically cohesive. A fix committed alongside a refactor cannot be cherry-picked cleanly. Teams that commit features as single atomic units spend far less time on backport conflicts.

questions.question: How do you use Git hooks to enforce code quality in a Java backend project?
questions.title: Git hooks for enforcing code quality
questions.direct_answer: Git hooks are shell scripts that run automatically at specific points in the Git workflow. In Java projects, a pre-commit hook can run Checkstyle or Spotless to reject poorly formatted code before it is committed, a commit-msg hook can enforce Conventional Commits message format, and a pre-push hook can run the test suite. Manage hooks with core.hooksPath to share them across the team via the repository.
questions.interviewer_intent: Assesses knowledge of shift-left quality practices, automation, and the candidate's ability to improve team code standards systematically rather than relying on manual review alone.

sections.title: The Fastest Code Review Comment Is the One That Never Gets Written
sections.content:
On teams without automated formatting checks, 20–30% of code review comments are about import ordering, brace placement, and naming conventions. These comments are tedious to write, tedious to read, and tedious to fix — and they slow down the review cycle for the actual logic. Git hooks eliminate this entire category of review friction by catching style violations before code even leaves the developer's machine.

**Git hooks** are executable scripts that live in `.git/hooks/` and fire at defined lifecycle events: `pre-commit` (before a commit is recorded), `commit-msg` (after the message is written but before the commit is finalized), `pre-push` (before a push is sent to the remote), and others. The challenge is that `.git/` is not tracked by Git, so hooks are not automatically shared across the team. The solution is committing hook scripts to a directory like `.githooks/` and configuring Git to use it with `core.hooksPath`.

The shift-left principle applies here: the earlier you catch a problem, the cheaper it is to fix. A formatting violation caught by a pre-commit hook costs the developer 5 seconds. The same violation caught in a code review costs the reviewer time to write the comment, the developer time to context-switch back, and the PR time waiting for re-review. Hooks are the highest-leverage quality investment a Java team can make.

sections.title: Share Hooks Across the Team With core.hooksPath and Build Tool Integration
sections.content:
The fundamental challenge with Git hooks is distribution — `.git/hooks/` is local and unversioned. Commit your hook scripts to `.githooks/` in the repository root and configure Git to use this directory.

For **Maven projects**, the `git-build-hook-maven-plugin` automates this during the build lifecycle. Adding the following plugin to your parent POM ensures that every developer who runs `mvn install` gets hooks configured automatically — the plugin sets `core.hooksPath` during the `initialize` phase.

```xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>com.rudikershaw.gitbuildhook</groupId>
  <artifactId>git-build-hook-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.5.0</version>
  <configuration>
    <gitConfig>
      <core.hooksPath>.githooks</core.hooksPath>
    </gitConfig>
  </configuration>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <goals><goal>configure</goal></goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
```

For Gradle, add a task that runs during project setup and make it a dependency of `compileJava`. Mark all scripts executable with `chmod +x .githooks/*` and commit that permission. The key principle: hook installation must be zero-effort — if developers have to run a manual setup command, adoption drops to near zero.

sections.title: Pre-commit: Kill Formatting Debates With Automated Checks
sections.content:
The `pre-commit` hook is the highest-value hook because it runs on every commit and catches the most common quality issues. Create `.githooks/pre-commit` as a shell script that runs Spotless or Checkstyle on staged files only — checking the entire repository on every commit would be too slow.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Only check staged Java files — keeps the hook under 5 seconds
STAGED=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep '\.java$')
if [ -z "$STAGED" ]; then
  exit 0  # No Java files staged, skip
fi
mvn spotless:check -q
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Formatting violations found. Run: mvn spotless:apply"
  exit 1
fi
```

The **5-second performance budget** is critical. Anything slower incentivizes developers to bypass the hook with `--no-verify`. Running checks only on staged files keeps the hook fast. If Spotless fails, the commit is aborted with a clear message telling the developer how to auto-fix.

For security-sensitive repositories, add a secrets scanner to the pre-commit hook using `gitleaks` or `detect-secrets`. This prevents accidental commits of API keys, database passwords, or certificates — a single committed secret in a public repo can be scraped within minutes by automated bots.

sections.title: commit-msg and pre-push: Message Standards and Test Gates
sections.content:
The `commit-msg` hook validates the commit message format before the commit is finalized. Enforcing **Conventional Commits** (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, etc.) enables powerful automation downstream — `semantic-release` can automatically determine version bumps, and `conventional-changelog` generates release notes from commit messages with zero human effort.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
MSG=$(cat "$1")
PATTERN='^(feat|fix|docs|refactor|test|chore|perf|ci)(\(.+\))?: .{10,}'
if ! echo "$MSG" | grep -qE "$PATTERN"; then
  echo "Invalid commit message format."
  echo "Expected: feat(scope): description (10+ chars)"
  exit 1
fi
```

The `pre-push` hook is the right place for heavier checks because pushes happen less frequently than commits. Run unit tests here: `mvn test -q`. If the full suite takes more than three minutes, scope it to changed modules using `git diff --name-only origin/main...` to identify affected directories, then run `mvn test -pl :changed-module`.

One critical caveat: **hooks are not security**. Any developer can bypass them with `--no-verify`. The hooks are a fast local feedback loop — the CI pipeline must mirror every hook check as the authoritative gate. Think of hooks as developer-friendly friction that catches issues before they waste CI time, not as an enforcement mechanism that can be trusted.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`core.hooksPath .githooks/` shares hooks via the repo** — commit hook scripts to `.githooks/` and automate installation through Maven/Gradle build plugins so every developer gets them on first build with zero manual setup
- **Pre-commit hook has a 5-second budget** — anything slower drives `--no-verify` bypass; run Spotless/Checkstyle only on staged `.java` files via `git diff --cached --name-only`
- **Conventional Commits in commit-msg unlock automation** — machine-parseable messages like `feat(auth):` enable `semantic-release` for automatic version bumps and `conventional-changelog` for generated release notes
- **Pre-push runs unit tests as a gate** — heavier than pre-commit but catches test failures before they waste CI minutes; scope to changed modules if the full suite exceeds 3 minutes
- **Hooks are not security — CI is the authoritative gate** — any developer can `--no-verify`; mirror every hook check in the pipeline so hooks are a fast feedback loop, not a trust boundary

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Git hooks run scripts automatically at defined points in the commit and push workflow — they catch quality issues at the earliest possible moment, before code leaves the developer's machine.

**Pre-commit hooks — the first quality gate**
- A Spotless or Checkstyle pre-commit hook formats and validates code before the commit is created; a developer never sees a CI failure for an import ordering issue or a missing newline — it is fixed locally in seconds
- Pre-commit hooks run on the staged files only, so they are fast — a format check on changed files takes under a second versus a full Maven build
- The `.git/hooks/` directory is not version-controlled; use the `git-build-hook-maven-plugin` or Husky (for Node-based projects) to automatically configure `core.hooksPath` during the build so every developer gets the same hooks without manual steps

**Commit-msg hooks — enforcing message conventions**
- A `commit-msg` hook validates the commit message against Conventional Commits format (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`) before the commit is recorded
- Conventional Commits enables automated changelog generation and semantic version bumping — tools like `semantic-release` parse commit history to determine whether the next version is a patch, minor, or major release
- The hook runs immediately after the developer types the message, giving instant feedback rather than a CI reviewer comment hours later

**The essential caveat: hooks are bypassable**
- Any developer can skip hooks with `git commit --no-verify` — hooks are a developer experience tool, not a security boundary
- Mirror every hook check in the CI pipeline as an authoritative gate; the hook catches issues in 5 seconds locally instead of 20 minutes in CI, but CI is what actually enforces the standard
- This layered approach — fast local feedback plus authoritative CI gate — is the right mental model for all quality automation
