questions.question: What are the trade-offs between a monorepo and a polyrepo strategy for Java backend services?
questions.title: Monorepo vs polyrepo strategies
questions.direct_answer: A monorepo stores all services and shared libraries in one repository, enabling atomic cross-service commits, easier refactoring, and unified tooling at the cost of slower CI and more complex build tooling. A polyrepo gives each service full autonomy and faster isolated pipelines at the cost of dependency versioning overhead and harder cross-service refactors. Most large Java organisations use a middle ground: a small number of repos grouped by domain or team ownership.
questions.interviewer_intent: Probes architectural decision-making, understanding of build tooling at scale (Gradle, Bazel, Maven), and experience with the organisational dynamics that influence repository structure.

sections.title: The Hidden Cost You Don't See Until the Cross-Cutting Refactor
sections.content:
Repository topology is as much an organizational decision as a technical one — Conway's Law predicts that your repo structure will mirror your team communication patterns, and vice versa. The decision feels abstract until the day you need to rename a field in a shared domain event that eight Java microservices consume.

In a **monorepo**, that rename is one PR, one CI run, one review — the change is atomic across all consumers. In a **polyrepo**, it is eight coordinated PRs across eight repositories, each of which must be merged in the right order to avoid breaking deployed services. At scale, that coordination cost is enormous and grows quadratically with the number of consuming services.

But polyrepos have a corresponding advantage that monorepos struggle with: team autonomy. A payments team should not need to wait for the notifications team to fix a failing test before they can merge a critical security patch. With separate repositories, each team's CI is a closed system, and build times stay fast because you are only building what that specific service needs.

The real question is not "monorepo or polyrepo" but "where do you draw the repository boundaries" — and the answer depends on how often your services change together versus independently.

sections.title: Monorepo vs Polyrepo: The Full Trade-off Matrix
sections.content:
The comparison reveals that each strategy optimizes for a different organizational priority — shared evolution versus independent autonomy.

| Dimension | Monorepo | Polyrepo |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-service refactors | Atomic — one PR touches all consumers | Coordinated PRs across repos, merged in order |
| Shared library versioning | Always on latest — no version drift | Each service pins a version; drift is common |
| CI build time | Slow without build caching (Gradle/Bazel) | Fast — each repo builds in isolation |
| Team autonomy | Requires coordination on tooling and CI config | Full independence per team |
| Dependency visibility | Complete dependency graph in one place | Cross-repo dependencies opaque without tooling |
| Access control | All-or-nothing without CODEOWNERS/sparse checkout | Independent permissions per repo |
| Onboarding | Clone once, see everything | Must clone and configure multiple repos |

sections.title: The Middle Ground: Domain-Grouped Repositories
sections.content:
The teams that succeed at scale rarely use pure monorepo or pure polyrepo — they use **domain-grouped repositories**. The payments domain lives in one repo with its three closely related services and their shared library. The notifications domain lives in another. This gives you most of the atomic-refactor benefit within a domain while keeping cross-domain coupling explicit and intentional.

For Java specifically, **Gradle's composite builds** feature is the key enabler for monorepo and domain-grouped strategies. It lets you define multiple `settings.gradle` projects in one repository and have them reference each other as source dependencies rather than published artifacts. You get the developer experience of "change the library, rebuild the consumer immediately" without waiting for a Maven publish cycle. Combine with Gradle's remote build cache and you eliminate the "monorepo builds are slow" problem — unchanged modules pull results from cache in seconds.

For polyrepo teams, invest in **Renovate or Dependabot** for automated dependency updates, and publish shared libraries to an internal artifact registry (Nexus, Artifactory) with semantic versioning. Version drift is the silent killer of polyrepo architectures — a shared library at v1.3 in one service and v1.1 in another means two services interpret the same domain event differently. Automated PRs that bump dependency versions keep services converged without manual coordination.

The decision framework: if your services change together more than 30% of the time (shared domain events, API contracts, schema migrations), group them in one repo. If they change independently more than 70% of the time, separate repos give more autonomy for less coordination cost.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The monorepo versus polyrepo decision changes fundamentally depending on the cost you are optimizing for: cross-cutting changes and dependency consistency, or team autonomy and build isolation.

**Monorepo — atomic cross-cutting changes**
- Renaming a field in a shared domain event consumed by eight services is one PR in a monorepo — the consumer changes compile, tests run, and the refactor merges atomically; in a polyrepo it requires eight coordinated PRs merged in dependency order
- Dependency versions are consistent across all services by definition — no service silently runs a different Jackson or Spring Boot version than the others, eliminating a class of subtle runtime incompatibility bugs
- The build tooling investment is real: Gradle composite builds, Bazel, or Nx are required to avoid rebuilding every service on every change; without incremental builds, a monorepo becomes slower with every service added

**Polyrepo — team autonomy and isolated CI**
- A payments team should not wait for the notifications team's failing test before merging a security patch — separate repositories give each team a closed CI system with independent build and deploy pipelines
- Service boundaries are explicit at the repository level; the coupling between teams is visible because it shows up as a versioned dependency, not an implicit shared file
- Renovate or Dependabot automates dependency version updates across repositories, reducing the manual coordination cost for keeping shared library versions aligned

**The pragmatic middle ground**
- Domain-grouped repositories organize related services together: the payments domain owns its API, worker, and shared library in one repo; the notifications domain owns its services in another
- Gradle composite builds let sibling projects reference each other as source dependencies rather than published artifacts — a library change triggers an immediate recompile of the consumer without a publish step

Draw repository boundaries along domain lines, not service lines. One repo per bounded domain, shared platform tooling in a separate repo that all domains consume.

questions.question: How do you use git bisect to find the commit that introduced a bug in a Java backend service?
questions.title: Git bisect for finding the commit that introduced a bug
questions.direct_answer: Git bisect performs a binary search through commit history to find the first commit where a condition changed — typically where a bug was introduced. You mark one commit as good (bug absent) and one as bad (bug present), and Git checks out the midpoint. You test it, mark it good or bad, and repeat until Git identifies the exact offending commit. The process takes O(log n) steps — finding the culprit in 1000 commits takes about 10 steps.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests systematic debugging skills and knowledge of advanced Git tooling that most developers underuse. Shows the candidate can diagnose production regressions efficiently without requiring full code review of every commit.

sections.title: Binary Search on History: 10 Steps to Find a Bug in 1000 Commits
sections.content:
Production regressions in Java services often arrive as "it worked last week" bugs with no obvious culprit. A Monday morning alert fires, the bug was not present on Friday, and 80 commits were merged over the weekend. Manually reviewing 80 diffs is a multi-hour task with no guarantee of finding the cause. **`git bisect`** automates this search with a binary search algorithm that halves the suspect range at each step.

The math is compelling: for 1000 commits, bisect needs at most 10 steps (log₂ 1000 ≈ 10). For 80 weekend commits, it needs about 7 steps. At each step, Git checks out the midpoint commit, you test whether the bug is present, and Git narrows the range. The tool is especially powerful when combined with an automated test — `git bisect run` hands the entire process to Git for zero-touch bisection.

The key prerequisite is that you can **distinguish a good state from a bad state** in a reproducible way. An automated test is ideal, but a manual curl command, a visual check, or any deterministic verification works. Without a reproducible test, bisect becomes a guessing game at each midpoint.

sections.title: Define the Search Range: One Good Commit, One Bad Commit
sections.content:
Start the bisect session with `git bisect start`. Then mark the boundaries of your search.

Mark the current broken state as bad: `git bisect bad HEAD` (or a specific SHA if HEAD isn't the broken version). Mark the last known good state: `git bisect good v2.3.0` — this can be a tag, a branch, or any commit SHA where you're confident the bug was absent. **Release tags** are ideal good markers because they represent tested, deployed states.

Git immediately computes the midpoint and checks out that commit. Your working tree changes to reflect the historical state — your Spring Boot application is now at a past version. This is non-destructive; Git will restore your original state when bisect ends.

A common mistake here is choosing a good boundary that's too recent. If the bug was introduced three weeks ago but you only go back one week, bisect will report a false result. When in doubt, go further back — the binary search means the extra commits add very few additional steps. Going from 100 commits to 200 adds only one more step.

sections.title: Test Each Midpoint — Or Automate With git bisect run
sections.content:
With Git checked out at the midpoint, run your reproducer: build the project, start the service, and execute the specific test that demonstrates the bug. If the bug is present, run `git bisect bad`. If absent, run `git bisect good`. Git immediately checks out the next midpoint and prints how many revisions remain.

The real power comes from **full automation** with `git bisect run`. If you have a test that returns exit code 0 for good and non-zero for bad, Git handles the entire binary search unattended. The following example runs a specific Maven test at each midpoint, marking good and bad boundaries before handing control to Git.

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v2.3.0
git bisect run mvn test -pl pricing-service \
  -Dtest=PricingCalculationTest -q
```

Git runs the Maven test at each midpoint, following the binary search to completion automatically. On a recent Java project, this found a `BigDecimal` rounding mode change buried in a dependency upgrade — the kind of regression that's nearly invisible in a code review but immediately obvious to a targeted test.

If a midpoint commit doesn't compile (common in a busy repo), use `git bisect skip` to tell Git to try adjacent commits instead. The search continues around the untestable commit. For `bisect run`, return exit code 125 from your script to signal "skip this commit" programmatically.

sections.title: Read the Verdict, Then Write the Regression Test Before Fixing
sections.content:
When bisect converges, Git prints the exact offending commit: its SHA, author, timestamp, and full commit message. Examine the diff with `git show <sha>` to understand what changed and why. Often the commit is a dependency upgrade, a refactor with an unintended side effect, or a configuration change — not an obvious bug.

End the bisect session with `git bisect reset`, which restores your working tree to the original HEAD. Now you have the full context: the exact change, the author to consult, and the rationale from the commit message.

**Before writing the fix, write the regression test.** Create a test that specifically exercises the broken behavior and fails against the current code. This serves two purposes: it verifies your fix actually addresses the root cause (not a symptom), and it permanently guards against the same regression returning. In a Java codebase, name the test explicitly — `PricingRoundingRegressionTest` — so future developers understand why it exists.

For particularly tricky regressions, use `git bisect log` to export the bisect session as a replayable script. Save it in the PR description or a project wiki. This documents your debugging process for the team and creates a runbook for similar investigations in the future.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Binary search halves the suspect range each step** — finding a bug in 1000 commits takes ~10 tests, making it practical to diagnose weekend merge floods that would take hours to review manually
- **`git bisect run` automates the entire loop** — supply a command that exits 0 for good and non-zero for bad; Git walks the commit range unattended and reports the exact first bad commit
- **Exit code 125 means skip** — when a midpoint commit doesn't compile, return 125 from your test script so bisect tries adjacent commits instead of treating the broken build as the bug
- **Write the regression test before the fix** — verify your fix addresses the root cause, not a symptom, and permanently guard against the same regression returning in a future refactor
- **Always `git bisect reset` to restore HEAD** — bisect leaves you in a detached HEAD state at the bad commit; reset returns to your original branch so you can write the fix

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Git bisect runs a binary search across commit history to find which commit introduced a regression. It is the correct tool when a bug exists in the current HEAD, did not exist at some known-good point, and reading 80 commits of diff would take hours.

**The binary search workflow**
- Mark a known-bad commit: `git bisect bad HEAD`; mark a known-good commit: `git bisect good v2.4.0`; bisect checks out the midpoint commit for you to test
- Test the checked-out version — compile, run the failing test, or hit the endpoint — then tell bisect `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`; it halves the remaining search space and checks out the next midpoint
- Seven rounds of bisection cover 128 commits; finding the culprit among 80 weekend commits takes about 7 rounds instead of reading all 80 diffs

**Automating bisect with a test script**
- `git bisect run mvn test -pl :order-service -Dtest=OrderServiceTest` automates the entire bisection — bisect runs the command at each midpoint and treats exit code 0 as good, non-zero as bad
- The test must be deterministic; a flaky test produces a false bad result that misdirects bisect to an innocent commit
- Write the reproduction test before starting bisect — having a precise, isolated test is what makes automation possible and the result reliable

**After finding the culprit commit**
- `git bisect reset` returns the repository to the original HEAD after the search completes
- Examine the identified commit with `git show <sha>` — the diff will be small (bisect found a specific commit, not a range) and the bug is usually obvious in context
- `git log --oneline <good>..<bad>` lists all commits in the bad range if you want to understand what changed in that window before bisect narrows it down
